strengths: The proposed method (is-QN) is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: storing only the final linear layer as a 'target' while sharing the feature extractor with the online network is a natural middle ground between target-based and target-free approaches, and the connection to iterated Q-learning is well explained.

The experimental evaluation is reasonably thorough for the claims made: online Atari (CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm), an offline RL setting with CQL, an ablation over the number of heads K, and an additional variant (ES-CQL) showing the sharing idea generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning.

The analysis section (Section 5.3) goes beyond raw performance numbers, using gradient cosine similarity and effective rank (srank) to explain WHY the method works, which strengthens the paper's scientific contribution.

The method achieves the stated practical goal: closing most of the target-free/target-based performance gap (and even surpassing the target-based baseline with K=9) while using roughly half the parameters and comparable training time.

Hyperparameters, game selection, AUC computation, and design choices (e.g., action sampling from heads, loss aggregation) are documented in detail in the appendix, supporting reproducibility; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially a combination of two existing ideas — copying the last linear layer as target (closely related to prior target-free/functional regularization work) and iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025) — applied to DQN and CQL. The conceptual step beyond these prior works is modest.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only discrete-control Atari benchmarks (15 games online, 10 offline), 5 seeds per experiment, and only DQN/CQL as base algorithms. No continuous control, no distributed/large-scale settings, and no demonstration on the high-dimensional-state or multi-input applications that motivate the memory-footprint argument in the introduction.

The claim that the approach is 'orthogonal' to regularization techniques for target-free methods is asserted but only weakly tested (BatchNorm is examined and rejected); comparisons with other target-free baselines (e.g., MellowMax, functional regularization, gradient-TD style methods) are absent, making it hard to judge is-QN's standing among target-free alternatives.

Several empirical observations are explained post-hoc with conjectures rather than validated claims (e.g., why K=49 underperforms with CNN but helps with IMPALA; the LayerNorm interplay), and these conjectures are not experimentally verified.

Some benefits are modest or setting-dependent: the improvement over TF-DQN without LayerNorm still leaves a residual 15-18% gap, and per-game curves show a few games (e.g., Asterix, VideoPinball) where the method does not help; the '6% improvement over the target-based approach' claim rests on a relatively small margin with overlapping uncertainty in places.

strengths: The proposed method (iterating Shared Q-learning, iS-QN) is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: storing only the last linear layer as a target head while sharing all other parameters with the online network is a natural, low-memory middle ground between target-based and target-free approaches.

The paper convincingly leverages the iterated Q-learning idea of Vincent et al. (2025) to boost target-free learning speed, and the experimental results are consistent across multiple settings (online DQN with CNN and IMPALA architectures, offline CQL, with and without LayerNorm), with proper use of IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, and AUC-based sample-efficiency metrics following Agarwal et al. (2021).

The analysis section (Section 5.3) goes beyond raw performance: gradient cosine-similarity and effective-rank (srank) analyses provide mechanistic insight into why sharing features and learning parallel Bellman iterations helps.

The variant comparison (Ensemble Shared Features vs. iterated Shared Features) demonstrates the idea of linear-head parameter sharing generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning, and the appendix is thorough (hyperparameters, per-game curves, game selection rationale, dormant neuron analysis).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a straightforward combination of two existing ideas—parameter sharing between target and online networks (well explored in prior target-free/functional-regularization work) and iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025). The delta over i-QN is reducing 2K networks to one network with K+1 linear heads, which is an architectural compression rather than a new algorithmic insight.

Narrow empirical scope: evaluation is restricted to discrete control on a subset of 10-15 Atari games with only 5 seeds per game, and only DQN/CQL. No continuous control, no non-Atari domains, and no challenging high-dimensional benchmarks despite the paper's motivation emphasizing large networks and scaling (e.g., mixtures of experts, multimodal inputs).

Claims of orthogonality to regularization techniques (MellowMax, functional regularization, BatchNorm, etc.) are asserted but not experimentally validated: no experiment combines iS-QN with these methods, so the claim that the approach can 'build on these to benefit from their performance gains' is unsupported.

The central efficiency claims are not fully substantiated: memory savings are shown, but there are no wall-clock/compute measurements or FLOP comparisons for the additional forward/backward passes through K heads, and the abstract's claim of 'comparable training time' lacks reported evidence.

Several design choices are under-ablated: the uniform head-sampling action-selection rule is inherited rather than studied in this shared setting, the loss aggregation choice is deferred to future work, and there is no analysis of sensitivity to the target update period T interacting with K (the assumption theta_{k-1} ~ theta_k for k << T is only informally argued).

Performance at large K is inconsistent across architectures (K=49 hurts with CNN but helps with IMPALA), and the explanation ('richer representation') is speculative; this suggests the method's benefit depends on architecture in a way the paper does not fully characterize.
Comparison against stronger target-free baselines or state-of-the-art target-free methods (beyond vanilla TF-DQN) is missing, making it hard to judge practical significance of the improvements.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the memory overhead of target networks limits Q-network scaling, and the paper offers a principled middle ground between target-based and target-free methods by storing only the final linear layer as the target while sharing all other parameters with the online network.

The method is simple, easy to implement (Algorithm 1), and elegantly combines two existing ideas—parameter sharing between target/online networks and iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025)—into a coherent algorithm (iS-QN) with negligible parameter overhead relative to target-based methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: online discrete control (CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm), offline RL (CQL variant), ablations over the number of heads K, and an additional variant (ES-CQL) demonstrating the idea generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning.

Good statistical practice: IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals, AUC normalized to the target-based baseline to measure sample efficiency, per-game learning curves in the appendix, and a principled game-selection procedure that is documented.

The analysis section (Section 5.3) is a genuine strength: gradient cosine similarity, effective rank (srank), and dormant neuron measurements provide mechanistic insight into why the method reduces the target-free performance gap, rather than only reporting aggregate scores.
Hyperparameters are kept identical to standard DQN settings, and the code is stated to be open-sourced, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the paper is essentially a combination of target-free feature sharing (Bhatt et al., 2024; Gallici et al., 2025) and iterated Q-Network (Vincent et al., 2025). While the synthesis is sensible, each ingredient is established, and the contribution is more engineering than conceptual breakthrough.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only discrete-action Atari (15 games for CNN, 10 for IMPALA) and one offline setting. Continuous control and other domains are deferred to future work, limiting claims of generality. The reduced game subsets (motivated by compute) raise concerns about selection effects on reported AUC gains.

The number of seeds (5 per game) is on the low side for Atari, where inter-seed variance is high; several reported improvements (e.g., the 6% AUC gain over TB-DQN with K=9) have overlapping confidence intervals in some figures.

The claim of 'comparable training time' is asserted but not substantiated with wall-clock or FLOPs measurements; learning K Bellman iterations per update adds non-trivial compute (K forward/backward passes through the shared torso), which is a practical cost the paper under-emphasizes.

Orthogonality to other target-free stabilization techniques (MellowMax, functional regularization, BatchNorm) is claimed but not empirically demonstrated via combinations; only LayerNorm is actually integrated. The BatchNorm comparison is limited to 5 games.

Performance degrades for large K on the CNN architecture (K=49) and the explanation ('shared feature representation not rich enough') is speculative; a deeper characterization of when the method helps or hurts is missing.

No theoretical grounding: the paper provides no analysis of why chaining Bellman targets through a shared, continuously-updating representation remains stable, which is the core question raised by the approach.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practical: storing only the last linear layer of the online network as the target drastically reduces the memory footprint of target-based Q-learning while recovering most of its benefit, and it composes cleanly with iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025) to further speed up learning.

Evaluation is broad and unusually thorough for this kind of method paper: online discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA), offline RL (CQL on Atari), continuous control (SAC on DMC-Hard with SimbaV2), and even an LLM-based offline RL task (ILQL on Wordle), with IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, multiple seeds, and per-game curves in the appendix.

The paper goes beyond raw benchmark results and provides a genuine analysis of why the method works: gradient cosine similarity to the target-based loss, target churn measurements, and srank/dormant-neuron analyses give a coherent picture of the improved learning dynamics.

Positioning against related work is careful: the authors explicitly contrast their approach with regularization-based target-free methods, gradient-TD methods, and prior chaining/iterated Q-learning work, and demonstrate the idea generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning (Ensemble Shared Features in Figure 5).

Reproducibility appears strong: full hyperparameter tables, code promised as supplementary, detailed setup descriptions, and honest reporting of training time/FLOPs including cases where the method does not reduce compute.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The 'Shared Features' idea (K=1) is a very small modification—freezing a copy of the last linear layer—and the main contribution is the combination with iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. (2025). Readers may see this as an incremental delta over existing work rather than a new mechanism.

There is no theoretical grounding. Prior work (Schmitt et al., 2022) provided convergence guarantees for chaining in the linear case; this paper is purely empirical and offers no analysis of when shared features can or cannot support K consecutive Bellman iterations, despite the authors' own conjecture that the shared representation may be a bottleneck at K=49.

The optimal number of heads K varies across settings (K=3, 9, or 49 depending on architecture and task), introducing a new hyperparameter without a principled selection rule; the paper acknowledges this but only notes that 'none of the values lead to a dramatic performance drop,' which weakens the practical recipe.

Benchmark coverage, while broad, is still restricted: 15 Atari games (reduced to 10 for the IMPALA experiments) and 7 DMC-Hard tasks are small subsets of the standard suites, and some results (e.g., iS-SAC K=9 vs. K=1 on DMC with discounted loss scaling) show the method's benefit can vanish under certain dynamics.

The memory-saving claim, while valid for Q-network parameters, is somewhat overstated in motivation: replay buffers and optimizer state often dominate RAM, as the authors themselves concede in the limitations section, and training time/FLOPs are not reduced (and are worse for the language task in some comparisons).
Several empirical claims rest on conjecture rather than evidence (e.g., why IMPALA tolerates K=49 but the CNN does not), and ablations on alternative loss aggregations are deferred to future work.

strengths: The core idea (storing only the last linear layer as a 'target head' while sharing all other parameters with the online network) is simple, well-motivated, and directly addresses a real practical concern: the memory overhead of target networks, which is relevant for edge devices and large-network settings.

The evaluation is unusually broad and thorough for this type of method: online discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures), offline RL (CQL on 10% DQN replay datasets), continuous control (SAC on 7 DMC Hard tasks with SimbaV2), and even language RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2). This demonstrates the idea is not tied to one setting or architecture.

The analysis section (Section 5.5) goes beyond aggregate performance: gradient cosine similarity to the target-based loss, target churn measurements, and effective rank (srank) of penultimate features give concrete, mechanistic insight into why sharing features helps, rather than only reporting curves.

The paper is honest about limitations (K as a new hyperparameter, no training-time reduction, orthogonal to regularization techniques) and reports memory/FLOPs/training time in a dedicated appendix (Figure 10), which supports the memory-efficiency claim rather than leaving it asserted.
Reproducibility appears strong: code promised as supplementary material, full hyperparameter tables, per-game learning curves, and clear description of the AUC/IQM metric computation.

The paper correctly positions itself as orthogonal to prior target-free regularization work (MellowMax, Fourier features, BatchNorm/CrossQ) and includes some of these as comparisons or ablations (e.g., BatchNorm degrading discrete-action performance).
weaknesses: Novelty is modest: the method is essentially the composition of two existing ideas — reusing online features for the target (related to functional regularization / target-free methods) and iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025) — with the main new technical content being the frozen linear-head design and the head-shift schedule. No theoretical analysis or convergence argument is provided.

The benchmark coverage is narrower than it first appears: only 15/10 Atari games per setting, 5-10 seeds, and 7 DMC Hard tasks. Given that target-network effects are known to be high-variance and game-dependent, the headline claims (e.g., 'outperforms target-based by 6%') rest on relatively small game subsets selected by the authors, which risks selection effects.

The optimal K varies across settings (1, 3, 9, or 49 depending on the experiment) and the paper offers only conjectures for why (e.g., shared representation not rich enough for K=49 on CNN, discounting factor explaining SAC behavior). This means practitioners face an unexplained hyperparameter choice without principled guidance, and no sensitivity study on other axes (e.g., target update period T) is provided.

Missing comparisons: the paper claims orthogonality to target-free regularization techniques but does not evaluate iS-QN combined with them (e.g., iS-DQN + MellowMax or Fourier features), nor against the strongest recent target-free baselines under identical budgets; the claim that the method 'bridges the gap' would be more convincing with such combinations.

The Wordle/ILQL experiment is a single niche language task, and the target-free baseline performs nearly on par with the target-based one there (as the authors themselves note), which weakens the generality of the 'bridging the gap' narrative in that setting.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., 'iS-DQN K=9 outperforms the target-based approach by 6%' is within overlapping confidence intervals in parts of the curves, and several per-game plots (e.g., Breakout, MsPacman) show the proposed method clearly below the target-based baseline.
The Ensemble Shared Features variant (ES-CQL) is introduced and evaluated only in the offline setting without much analysis of when a chain (iS) versus an ensemble (ES) structure should be preferred.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated idea: storing only the last linear layer as a 'target' while sharing all other parameters elegantly interpolates between target-free (K-shifted every step) and target-based (window shifted every T steps) approaches, and reinterpreting the target-free method as an extreme case of this framing is insightful.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across four distinct settings (online discrete control with DQN/CNN and IMPALA, offline CQL, continuous control with SAC on DMC-hard, and offline RL on language models with ILQL/GPT-2), with sound statistical methodology (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC metric).

Results are convincing: the proposed method substantially reduces or eliminates the target-free vs. target-based performance gap, and in several settings (Atari CNN K=9, DMC humanoid, Wordle) even outperforms the target-based baseline while using roughly half the parameters.
Useful mechanistic analysis (gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank/srank, dormant neurons) that goes beyond aggregate scores and supports the claims about why the method works.

Good related work coverage and clear positioning relative to iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025), regularization-based target-free methods, and gradient temporal-difference approaches; the ensemble variant (ES-CQL) shows the idea generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning.
Hyperparameters are kept from the original algorithms without re-tuning, and the reproducibility statement, hyperparameter tables, and per-game curves in the appendix are thorough.
weaknesses: The core contribution is technically simple/incremental: freezing a copy of the last linear layer is a small modification of DQN, and the second component is directly borrowed from iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025); the novelty rests mainly on the combination and the empirical study.

Memory savings are only about 50% of Q-network parameters in most experiments, not the near-target-free footprint the framing might suggest; for small networks the absolute savings are modest, and the method does not reduce FLOPs or training time (Section B).

No theoretical analysis; the convergence properties of learning K chained Bellman iterations against a shared, drifting feature extractor are unexamined, and the explanation for why large K degrades on the CNN but not IMPALA architecture remains speculative ('conjecture').

Evaluation uses reduced subsets of benchmarks (15/10 Atari games instead of the full 57, 7 DMC tasks) justified by compute budget, which weakens the generality of the headline claims; some per-game curves (e.g., VideoPinball, Breakout, MsPacman) show notable variance or underperformance.
K is a new hyperparameter whose optimal value varies across settings (K=1 vs. 3 vs. 9 vs. 49), and the paper offers limited practical guidance for selecting it despite acknowledging this limitation.

The claim that the method is orthogonal to existing target-free regularization techniques is asserted, but the main experiments do not directly evaluate combinations with those techniques (only LayerNorm/BatchNorm are used), so the composability claim is not empirically substantiated.

Several favorable comparisons rely on normalized AUC relative to the target-based baseline; reporting final performance and absolute scores alongside would make the practical significance easier to judge.

strengths: The proposed method (iterated Shared Q-Learning) is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: storing only the last linear layer as a 'target' while sharing all other parameters with the online network is an elegant, low-memory middle ground between target-free and target-based approaches.

Unusually broad empirical coverage for an RL paper: online discrete control (Atari with two architectures), offline RL (CQL), continuous control (DMC-hard with SAC/SimbaV2), language-model RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2), and streaming RL, consistently showing gap reduction between target-free and target-based variants.
Section 5.6 provides a genuine attempt at understanding *why* the method works (gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank/srank), which goes beyond pure benchmarking.

Good use of modern evaluation practices: IQM with stratified bootstrap CIs (Agarwal et al.), normalized AUC, ablations on K, target update period T, architecture width, MellowMax combination, meta-gradient coefficient tuning, and a mixed-precision pilot study.
Strong reproducibility: code is shared with exact dependencies, hyperparameters are exhaustively listed, individual learning curves are provided, and carbon impact is reported.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially a combination of two existing ideas — sharing parameters between target and online networks, and iterated Q-Network (Vincent et al., 2025b), which appears to be from the same group. The core contribution is an architectural tweak (freezing only the last linear layer) rather than a new principle.

The method does not consistently beat target-based baselines; the claim is carefully limited to 'bridging the gap', and in several settings (SAC with K=9 vs K=1, streaming with K=9, offline CQL) gains are modest or absent, leaving the practical value of large K unclear.

Some experimental design choices weaken comparability: different normalization schemes (LayerNorm for DQN, BatchNorm for SAC, none for TB-SAC) are applied selectively per algorithm, partly justified post-hoc (Figure 21/25), which makes head-to-head comparisons harder to interpret.

Limited theoretical grounding: there is no analysis of when shared-feature targets should or should not work (e.g., relationship between feature drift and target quality), and the number of Bellman iterations K is a new hyperparameter with setting-dependent optima that must be tuned empirically.
The explanations in Section 5.6 (target churn, srank, gradient similarity) are correlational observations rather than validated causal accounts of the improvement.

Sample sizes are modest for some claims (3–5 seeds per run, subsets of 7–15 Atari games), and the paper does not compare against stronger target-free regularization baselines beyond MellowMax in the main text.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across five distinct RL settings (online discrete control with two architectures, offline RL with CQL, continuous control with SAC on DMC-hard, language RL with ILQL on GPT-2, and streaming RL), which goes well beyond the typical single-benchmark evaluation for algorithmic RL papers.

The proposed iS-QN is simple, well-motivated by a practical problem (memory footprint of target networks), and the memory/parameter analysis is concrete and quantified (e.g., ~50% parameter reduction on Atari, 88M parameters saved on the language task).

Good analysis section (Section 5.6): gradient cosine similarity, target churn, and effective rank (srank) measurements provide mechanistic insight into why the method works, rather than only reporting aggregate scores.

Solid experimental hygiene: IQM with stratified bootstrap CIs following Agarwal et al. (2021), multiple seeds, reported hyperparameters, ablations on K, target update period T, network width, MellowMax integration, and a mixed-precision pilot study.
Reproducibility statement, code release, full hyperparameter tables, and per-game learning curves in the appendix.
Honest limitation discussion, including that the training-time/FLOP savings are negligible and that inference memory is not reduced.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is a fairly direct combination of iterated Q-learning (Vincent et al., 2025b) with the idea of sharing features between online and target networks; the K=1 variant is essentially 'copy the last linear layer,' which is a very small modification to DQN. The main contribution is empirical rather than conceptual.

No theoretical grounding: there is no analysis of when frozen linear heads over shifting shared features constitute valid Bellman targets, or when the chained-iteration approximation holds; the paper relies entirely on empirical evidence.

Gains are inconsistent across settings: iS-SAC K=9 performs only on par with K=1 and merely matches (not exceeds) the target-based approach with overlapping CIs; streaming results are on only 7 games with K=9 not helping; some per-game curves (e.g., MsPacman, Breakout with CNN) show the method substantially below the target-based baseline.

The experimental protocol treats target-based and target-free baselines differently in some settings (e.g., BatchNorm for TF/iS but not TB in SAC; LayerNorm choices), which, while justified by the authors' ablations, complicates the interpretation of 'closing the gap' claims.
A new hyperparameter K with setting-dependent optima (1 to 49) is introduced; the tuning advice is heuristic and the benefits at large K depend on architecture richness, which limits generality.
Small numbers of seeds (3-5) and reduced game subsets for the IMPALA experiments weaken statistical power for the margin-above-threshold claims.
The framing as 'bridging the performance gap' slightly overstates: in several settings the gap is narrowed rather than closed, and the method does not reduce training time or FLOPs.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: reducing the memory footprint of target networks in deep RL while retaining their stabilizing benefits. The proposed 'Shared Features' idea (using a frozen copy of the last linear layer as the target) is simple, elegant, and easy to implement.

The combination with iterated Q-learning (multiple linear heads learning consecutive Bellman iterations in parallel) is a natural and well-motivated extension that improves sample efficiency of target-free methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad and covers online discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures), offline RL (CQL), online continuous control (SAC with SimbaV2 on DMC Hard), language-based RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)), which is well beyond what most papers in this space evaluate.

Good experimental hygiene: IQM with 95% stratified bootstrap CIs following Agarwal et al. (2021), multiple seeds, hyperparameters kept at standard values, ablations on K, target update period T, feature width, and comparison with MellowMax.

The analysis section is a genuine strength: gradient cosine similarity, the novel 'target churn' metric, and effective rank (srank) measurements provide mechanistic insight into why sharing features improves learning dynamics.

The method is shown to be orthogonal/composable with existing target-free techniques (LayerNorm, BatchNorm, MellowMax, mixed-precision training), and an 'Ensemble Shared Features' variant shows the idea generalizes beyond iterated Q-learning.

The paper is honest about limitations (new hyperparameter K, settings where larger K does not help, unchanged training time/FLOPs), and includes reproducibility statements, hyperparameter tables, and per-game learning curves in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core mechanism (frozen last linear layer over shared features) is a simple architectural modification, and the iterated component is directly imported from Vincent et al. (2025b). The main contribution is the combination plus empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Results are mixed in places and the narrative occasionally overstates them: iS-SAC K=9 performs only on par with K=1, iS-Stream Q(λ) K=9 is unhelpful in the streaming setting, and iS-DQN K=49 degrades on CNN but not IMPALA. The recommended hyperparameter selection strategy for K ('increase until performance decreases') is expensive and somewhat unsatisfying.

Claims of 'outperforming' the target-based approach (e.g., +6% AUC on Atari CNN) rest on relatively few seeds (5 per game) over 10-15 games; some confidence intervals overlap, and the advantage over TB baselines should be interpreted cautiously.

The normalization choice differs across settings (LayerNorm for discrete actions, BatchNorm only for target-free and iS variants in continuous control), which weakens the fairness of some head-to-head comparisons, even though the authors justify it empirically.

There are minor inconsistencies and editorial issues: e.g., Appendix C refers to 'the experiment on the language task (Section 6)' when it is Section 5.4; the 0.25 discounting factor on future loss terms introduced in Section 5.3 appears ad hoc and its interaction with the finding in D.4 that equal weights are optimal is not fully reconciled.

The memory-saving argument, while real for the Q-network parameters, is partially diluted by the observation that other components (replay buffer, optimizer state) often dominate RAM, and training time/FLOPs are not reduced except for ILQL.
No theoretical analysis is provided (even for the linear case, where results of Schmitt et al. (2022) might be adaptable), leaving the stability claims purely empirical.
